subject: Creativity
title: Personas: Fictional People, Real Insights
description: A 60-second lesson on Personas: Fictional People, Real Insights.

hook.text: Meet Sarah, 34, a nurse with two kids who has 12 minutes for lunch.

buildup.text: Personas are fictional characters based on real research — composite profiles that represent key user segments with.

discovery.text: Alan Cooper introduced personas in 1999 to stop teams from designing for themselves. 'We' isn't the user. Sarah is.

twist.text: Bad personas are demographic stereotypes. Good personas capture behaviors, frustrations, goals, and context — the stuff.

climax.text: When teams ask 'What would Sarah do?' instead of 'What do we think?

punchline.text: The best design decisions are made for imaginary people based on real ones.

quiz.question: Who introduced the concept of design personas?

details.summary: Personas are fictional characters built from real user research data. They give design teams a concrete person to design for rather than abstract demographics. A well-crafted persona has a name, face, goals, frustrations, and behaviors that guide every design decision.
details.whyItMatters: Personas prevent the common error of designing for yourself. They keep the real user present in every meeting, preventing feature creep and ensuring the solution serves actual human needs.
takeaways: Personas are fictional but based on real research data
They provide a concrete reference point for design decisions
Good personas include goals, frustrations, and behavioral patterns

faq.question: How many personas should a project have?
faq.answer: Three to five primary personas cover most user types without creating confusion. Too many personas dilute focus. A primary persona represents the most important user, with secondary personas ensuring edge cases are not ignored.

faq.question: Can personas be harmful?
faq.answer: Yes, if poorly constructed. Personas based on assumptions rather than research encode biases. Stereotypical personas that reduce users to demographics are worse than no personas at all. Good personas require genuine user research.
